A.explanation: The ball is only momentarily compressed and then regains its shape, so the deformation is elastic and not permanent.

B.explanation: The clinking sound shows a brief elastic vibration of the spoon and mug with no permanent change of shape described.

C.explanation: The plank remains bent after the toolbox load is removed, so it has kept a permanent extension beyond its elastic limit.

D.explanation: The weighing-scale spring is designed to compress under load and return to its original length when the person steps off, which is elastic behaviour.

hints: Look for the time words in each option: momentarily compressed in A versus no longer straight after removal in C.
Recall that elastic deformation is fully reversed when the load is removed, while plastic deformation leaves a permanent change of shape.
Test each case by asking: after the ball, spoon, plank and spring are unloaded, which one object is described as staying deformed.
walkthrough: State the rule: a material shows elastic deformation if it returns to its original shape when the deforming force is removed, and plastic deformation if part of the deformation remains.
Check the rubber ball in A: it is momentarily compressed on impact and then bounces back, so the shape change is reversed.
Check the spoon and mug in B and the bathroom-scale spring in D: both are intended to vibrate or compress under load and then recover, with no permanent bend described.
Check the plank with the toolbox in C: the load causes bending and when the toolbox is removed the plank is no longer straight, so a permanent set remains.
That permanent change after unloading matches the definition of being taken beyond the elastic limit into plastic deformation. This is option C.
